name: Charts

hero.title: A quarter of ECharts' weight. Up to 8.7× faster.
hero.lede: Write a chart as JSX: rows in, marks as children, field names checked against your row type. Axes, an accessible data table and a spoken description come without asking (the tooltip is one `<Tooltip />` child), on canvas in the browser, as SVG on the server, and natively on iOS and Android.

why.title: Charts that behave like the rest of your UI.

items.title: Marks are children
items.text: A combo chart is a `<Bar>` beside a `<Line>`. A second axis is `<Line axis="right">` plus `<Axis y2>`. Wrap a mark in `<Show>` and its series comes and goes with the signal.

items.title: Typos fail typecheck
items.text: `<Chart<Row>>` checks `x` against your row. Declare `const RowBar = Bar<Row>` once and every `y="revnue"` is a type error. It compiles to `Bar` itself, so it costs nothing.

items.title: Accessible without asking
items.text: Every chart renders an offscreen data table and an `aria-label` written from the data: "rising 45% from 100 to 145". Left and Right walk the points; Up and Down switch series.

items.title: Pay for what you draw
items.text: Each mark and family is an imported binding. A pie costs 19.1 KB gzipped (ECharts: 117.2 KB), and a chart without `<Toolbox>` carries no tool strip. CI import budgets keep it that way.

difference.title: The options object goes. The effect goes with it.

before.label: React + ECharts 6
before.caption: Register the pieces, init on a ref, resize by hand, dispose on unmount, and reshape your rows into parallel arrays on every change.

after.label: with @pyreon/charts
after.caption: Rows in, marks as children. Resizing, disposal and repaint on data change are the chart's job. Field names are checked.
after.code:
import { Axis, Bar, Chart, Legend, Line, Tooltip, currency } from '@pyreon/charts'

type Row = { month: string; revenue: number; target: number }
const RowBar = Bar<Row>
const RowLine = Line<Row>

export const Revenue = (props: { rows: Row[] }) => (
  <Chart<Row> data={props.rows} x="month" height={320}>
    <RowBar y="revenue" label="Revenue" />
    <RowLine y="target" label="Target" />
    <Axis y format={currency('$')} />
    <Tooltip />
    <Legend />
  </Chart>
)

demo.title: Swap the mark, keep the data.
demo.text: Same rows, different marks. In the package this is one JSX child changing, and the canvas repaints in place.
demo.referenceHtml:
mark
data
demo.spec: Mount a real @pyreon/charts <Chart> over eight monthly rows (revenue, users and a target line). The "mark" control swaps the first child between <Bar>, <Line>, <Area> and <Dot>; the "data" control switches its y field between revenue and users. The target stays a <Line dash={[5, 4]}> and the chart carries <Axis y>, <Tooltip> and <Legend>. Keep the code panel showing the exact JSX being rendered. Tab into the canvas and use the arrow keys to show that keyboard focus and the spoken description come for free.

features.title: A whole charting engine, and none of it borrowed.

items.name: Cartesian marks:
items.text: `Bar` (stacked, grouped, waterfall), `Line`, `Area`, `StackedArea`, `Dot` with area-mapped bubbles, `Band`, `Histogram`, error bars on every mark.

items.name: Indicators as marks:
items.text: `Sma`, `Ema`, `Trend` and `Bollinger` layer over the series they smooth.

items.name: Family marks:
items.text: `<Arc>` is a pie or donut, `<Stage>` a funnel, `<Cell>` a heatmap, `<Candle>` a candlestick. Same `<Chart>`, same grammar.

items.name: 16 family components:
items.text: Sankey, treemap, sunburst, tree, graph, chord, river, polar, radar, gauge, gantt, calendar, parallel, boxplot, single axis and GeoJSON maps.

items.name: Chrome as children:
items.text: `Axis`, `Scale`, `Tooltip`, `Legend`, `Zoom` and `Toolbox`. `Zoom` and `Toolbox` carry their own code, so a chart without them ships no zoom or tool strip.

items.name: Keyed updates:
items.text: `by="id"` makes bars and lines slide, grow in and shrink out by row, like `<For by>`.

items.name: One formatter, every surface:
items.text: `currency`, `percent`, `compact`, `fixed` and `date` feed the axis, the tooltip and the accessible table at once. `locale="de-DE"` switches to Intl.

items.name: Long data and small multiples:
items.text: `color="region"` pivots long-format rows into one series per value; `facet="region"` draws one panel per value on a shared y domain.

items.name: Big series:
items.text: M4 decimation before every stroke, `maxPoints` thins with LTTB. The engine's marks (`line`, `bars`) also take a `Float64Array` or `number[]` column, a plain `number[]` used without a copy, and `density="device"` trades detail for speed.

items.name: SVG on the server:
items.text: `chartToSvg` plus a serializer per family, from `@pyreon/charts/svg`. Deterministic output, so a snapshot test asserts geometry, not pixels.

api.title: 60 exports on the main entry. Two more entries for servers and tinkerers.

limits.title: Give the marks the row type too
limits.text: `<Chart<Row>>` checks the chart's own channels. JSX cannot pass a type argument down to children, so declare `const RowBar = Bar<Row>` once to check a mark's field names.

limits.title: iOS and Android are experimental
limits.text: The engine is generated into Swift and Kotlin and `<Chart>` draws natively. Column inputs, `density`, `locale`, `facet`, `<Histogram>` and the event props (`onSelect` taps do cross) stay on the web, and the compiler names each one.

limits.title: The server draws the first frame
limits.text: Import `@pyreon/charts/svg` on the server and every chart ships its first frame as SVG in the HTML. Tooltips, zoom and keyboard focus attach in the browser.

limits.title: Stay on the main entry
limits.text: `@pyreon/charts/engine` exposes every layout, hit test and the array form `<PlotChart>`. It is useful and it is outside the stability promise.

comingFrom.title: An option object becomes a mark.
comingFrom.note: `innerRadius={0.57}` is ECharts' `['40%', '70%']` as a fraction of the outer radius. The docs' migration table maps each series type to its mark: `bar` to `<Bar>`, `pie` to `<Arc>`, `markLine` to `<Rule>`, `dataZoom` to `<Zoom>`. On the four timed operations in the record, the same engine is 2.5–8.7× faster than ECharts 6 (one run).

comingFrom.title: Stop copying data into the chart.
comingFrom.note: No `register` list, no `chart.update()`: the chart reads the signal. `smooth` is a monotone cubic, so it never draws a peak the data does not have. Against Chart.js 4 with decimation, bar mounts are 2.11–2.23× faster and 100,000-point updates 1.44–1.45× (two runs); a 1,000,000-point mount with row objects is 1.16–1.20× slower.

export const Revenue = (props: { rows: Row[] }) => (

comingFrom.note: Recharts already composes with JSX, so the move is mostly renames: `dataKey` becomes `y`, `ComposedChart` becomes `<Chart>`, and `ResponsiveContainer` goes away because the chart fills its container. In the same run Recharts 3 took 644 ms to mount a 100,000-point line; the Pyreon engine took 5.77 ms.

recipes.title: A live chart that keeps the last minute
recipes.text: Push a reading every second and keep sixty. `by="t"` matches rows by key, so the line slides left instead of every point morphing into its neighbour.

recipes.title: Price and volume, zoomed together
recipes.text: One `createChartLink()` shares the zoom window between charts, and the crosshair too once each has `<Tooltip crosshair />`. The navigator strip and the preset buttons sit under the price chart.

recipes.title: A chart in an email
recipes.text: On a server there is no canvas. `chartToSvg` returns an SVG string with `role="img"` and a title, ready for an email, a PDF or a static page.
recipes.code:
import { chartToSvg } from '@pyreon/charts/svg'
import { bars, line } from '@pyreon/charts/engine'

type Row = { month: string; revenue: number; target: number }
const rows: Row[] = [
  { month: 'Jan', revenue: 3200, target: 3000 },
  { month: 'Feb', revenue: 4100, target: 3400 },
  { month: 'Mar', revenue: 3800, target: 3800 },
]

// A string, with no DOM: write it into an email, a PDF or a static page.
export const svg = chartToSvg({
  data: rows,
  x: (d) => d.month,
  marks: [bars((d: Row) => d.revenue, { label: 'Revenue' }), line((d: Row) => d.target, { label: 'Target' })],
  title: 'Monthly revenue',
  width: 640,
  height: 320,
})

faq.q: Is this a wrapper around ECharts?
faq.a: Not any more. It used to be. The engine that replaced it is plain TypeScript over a flat draw list, and the package depends on nothing outside Pyreon. The docs carry a table from ECharts options to marks, and `pyreon check` lists any import still on the old wrapper.

Canvas in the browser: one element, however many points. SVG on the server, from the same draw list, through `@pyreon/charts/svg`. Import that entry on the server and every `<Chart>` ships its first frame as SVG in the HTML.

Mounting a line from row objects: 1.17–1.20× behind uPlot at 10,000 points and 1.16–1.20× behind Chart.js at 1,000,000 (two runs). The columnar input coming in the next release (a `number[]` column instead of row objects) ties Chart.js at a million. Every Pyreon run also builds the accessible table, which the others skip.

faq.q: Does it run on iOS and Android?
faq.a: Yes, experimentally. The geometry is generated into Swift and Kotlin and compiled by the real toolchains on every change, and `<Chart>` and the family components lower to a native canvas over the same draw list. VoiceOver gets an Audio Graph through `AXChartDescriptor`. What stays web-only is named at compile time.
38.0 KB gzipped for a line chart and 19.1 KB for a pie, measured beyond an 11.2 KB Pyreon runtime baseline (overnight run). Tree-shaken ECharts: 155.9 KB and 117.2 KB.
They are author-run and synthetic, on one M3 Max. Every one comes with its run count, and the harness is in the repo: `bun bench-scenarios.ts --scenario charts` in `examples/benchmark`. Run it.
